Despite its historical role as a primary recognized cause of human aseptic meningitis, clinical detections have remained sparse in modern surveillance records, leading to diagnostic underestimation. The synthesis highlights how this mammarenavirus presents an expansive clinical spectrum, stretching from self-limiting febrile episodes to severe meningoencephalitis, serious congenital malformations, and fatal donor-derived infections among solid organ transplant recipients. At the molecular level, lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus is classified within the Arenaviridae family and genus Mammarenavirus, forming pleomorphic, enveloped virions measuring 110 to 130 nanometers in diameter with a characteristic sandy interior created by embedded host ribosomes. Its helical nucleocapsid encases an ambisense, single-stranded RNA genome partitioned into two segments designated short and large. The short segment encodes the nucleoprotein, which orchestrates viral transcription and replication, and the glycoprotein precursor cleaved into envelope subunits GP1 and GP2 plus a stable signal peptide. The large segment encodes the matrix zinc-binding protein and an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase. Cellular attachment is heavily governed by the interaction between GP1 and host alpha-dystroglycan, though binding affinities diverge widely across strains; high-affinity variants such as Clone 13, Traub, and WE54 demonstrate distinct tissue tropism and viral persistence in animal models, whereas low-affinity variants such as Armstrong, E350, and WE2.2 rely on alternative attachment factors, including heparan sulfate proteoglycans. The epidemiological maintenance of lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus relies fundamentally on the house mouse, Mus musculus, which sheds immense viral quantities across nasal secretions, saliva, milk, semen, urine, and feces when infected prenatally due to immune tolerance. Secondary rodent species, such as hamsters, rats, and guinea pigs, are also susceptible to infection, although their capacities to sustain prolonged maintenance cycles remain less established. Human transmission takes place through inhalation of aerosolized rodent excreta, handling of contaminated dust, food contamination, or direct animal bites, alongside vertical and donor-derived pathways. Lineages IV and V have been recorded in wild rodents within the Caucasus and Spain, while the divergent Dandenong virus was detected during an Australian transplant cluster. Current European epidemiological investigations reveal an extensive disparity between active viral circulation within reservoir communities and documented human clinical cases, a discrepancy largely driven by absent systematic surveillance, nonspecific symptom profiles, and the scarcity of routine diagnostic panels. Seroepidemiological research from Hungary exemplifies this gap: a retrospective analysis of seventy-four cerebrospinal fluid samples from individuals with central nervous system infections of unidentified origin identified confirmed infections in 2.7 percent of cases, while a subsequent national study spanning 2017 to 2023 documented twenty-three acquired cases and two serologically confirmed congenital infections. Similarly, a retrospective investigation in Piedmont, Italy, evaluating 371 serum samples from patients suspected of rodent-borne infections uncovered an IgG seroprevalence rate of 2.7 percent, demonstrating prior exposure despite absent clinical diagnoses. Seroepidemiologic studies have also recorded exposure in pregnant cohorts in Philadelphia, where IgG seropositivity reached 2.4 to 2.7 percent, alongside seropositivity reaching 13 percent in Austrian zoo workers, 36 percent in Croatian rodents, and 37.5 percent in Slovakian rodents. The mechanisms governing human neuropathogenesis remain incompletely understood and rely primarily on experimental observations gathered from adult mouse and neonatal rat models rather than direct human clinical investigations. Following initial peripheral transmission and systemic replication, the virus accesses the central nervous system, likely via endothelial infection and subsequent disruption of the blood-brain barrier. In adult rodent models, acute central nervous system disease is fundamentally driven by host immunopathology rather than direct cytolytic damage caused by viral replication. Specifically, virus-specific CD8+ T lymphocytes release potent chemokines that trigger massive infiltrations of inflammatory monocytes and neutrophils into meningeal tissues, precipitating vascular leakage and severe intracranial pathology. In neonatal rat paradigms, experimental findings reveal that viral strain characteristics dictate distinct cellular affinities; strain E350 preferentially infects glial structures, whereas WE2.2 and Clone 13 preferentially target neuronal populations. Clinically apparent infections in immunocompetent hosts typically follow a mild or moderate course, though a notable portion of patients experience a characteristic biphasic trajectory marked by initial systemic illness followed by a neurological phase after a temporary symptom-free window. When aseptic meningitis develops, lumbar puncture reveals marked lymphocytic pleocytosis, with white cell counts extending from one hundred to several thousand cells per microliter and lymphocytes constituting greater than 80 percent of the cellular population. Mild to moderate hypoglycorrhachia is frequently documented, occasionally declining to fifteen milligrams per deciliter, or 0.83 millimoles per liter. A smaller subset of patients progresses to meningoencephalitis characterized by altered mental status, seizures, or focal deficits, typically presenting with normal neuroimaging or nonspecific inflammatory patterns. In sharp contrast to the self-limiting course seen in immunocompetent individuals, donor-derived transmission in solid organ transplantation results in catastrophic clinical disease marked by rapid progression, multi-organ failure, and exceptionally high mortality. Worldwide surveillance has documented five distinct transplant clusters encompassing seventeen organ recipients who received kidneys, livers, or lungs from donors harboring unrecognized, transient viral infections. In the United States clusters recognized in 2003 and 2005, eight organ recipients contracted the pathogen, resulting in seven fatalities within nine to seventy-six days post-transplantation; epidemiological tracing in the 2005 event linked the donor to an infected domestic pet hamster carrying an identical lineage I strain. Subsequent transplant transmissions in Massachusetts in 2008 and nationally in 2011 caused four additional patient deaths. In Australia, the novel Dandenong lineage caused the deaths of three female organ recipients within four to six weeks following transplantation from an infected donor. Congenital transmission represents another devastating clinical manifestation of lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus, with eighty-eight confirmed fetal cases recorded in published medical literature since the first description in England in 1955. Maternal exposure during pregnancy, which frequently manifests as a transient or asymptomatic febrile episode, permits transplacental viral dissemination into the developing fetal central nervous system, particularly during early gestational trimesters. A comprehensive clinical review by Pencole and colleagues evaluating sixty-eight congenital cases demonstrated that manifestations are dominated by chorioretinitis in 84 percent of cases, hydrocephalus in 53 percent, microcephaly in 31 percent, ventriculomegaly in 16 percent, and periventricular calcifications in 16 percent. Extracerebral complications include fetal growth restriction, hydrops fetalis, cardiomegaly, ascites, and anemia. Case records, such as an infection following a mouse bite at six weeks of gestation leading to extensive bilateral ventriculomegaly and termination at twenty-two weeks, underscore the critical necessity of including the virus within differential diagnoses for unexplained TORCH-negative congenital neuropathies. Establishing a reliable diagnosis demands a strategic multimodal approach tailored to the infection stage, as clinical signs overlap substantially with other infectious entities and commercially approved tests remain exceedingly rare. Molecular diagnosis using reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction serves as the primary method during early acute viremia and neuroinvasive phases, targeting conserved sequences within the nucleoprotein, large protein, or short genomic segment. A recently validated quantitative assay targeting the short segment demonstrated an analytical limit of detection of 5.6 genome copies per microliter across all five viral lineages. Serological evaluation utilizing enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays and indirect immunofluorescence assays evaluates IgM and IgG antibodies, though single IgM determinations remain merely presumptive and require confirmation via paired sera demonstrating significant titer elevations. Diagnosticians must also navigate cross-reactivity with related mammarenaviruses and recognize that antibody responses are frequently absent in immunosuppressed transplant recipients. Culturing replication-competent virus in BHK-21, L-929, or Vero cells remains limited to research facilities due to weak cytopathic effects and specialized BSL-3 or ABSL-3 containment requirements. Therapeutic options for human infection remain strictly supportive, as no antiviral agents or protective human vaccines have demonstrated definitive efficacy in controlled clinical trials. For uncomplicated meningitis cases, clinical management focuses on analgesia, hydration, and monitoring, while transplantation-associated disease requires urgent reduction of pharmacological immunosuppression accompanied by individualized salvage regimens involving the broad-spectrum guanosine analogue ribavirin. Preclinical evaluations have identified several direct-acting antiviral candidates, including the nucleoside analogues favipiravir, 4′-fluorouridine, and its orally available prodrug VV251, along with cap-dependent endonuclease inhibitors and monoclonal neutralizing antibodies targeting viral surface glycoproteins. Because therapeutic measures remain restricted, public health strategies emphasize primary prevention through comprehensive rodent control programs, safe disposal of household infestations using wet cleaning techniques to suppress airborne aerosols, and the utilization of personal protective equipment. Furthermore, enhanced One Health epidemiological surveillance and rigorous donor exposure questionnaires are imperative to mitigate transmission risks across vulnerable obstetric and organ transplant populations worldwide. analysis_zh.location_and_population: 在高加索和西班牙的野生啮齿动物中已记录到 IV 和 V 谱系,而在澳大利亚移植集群中检测到了不同的丹德农病毒。
analysis_zh.event: Seroepidemiologic studies have also recorded exposure in pregnant cohorts in Philadelphia, where IgG seropositivity reached 2.4 to 2.7 percent, alongside seropositivity reaching 13 percent in Austrian zoo workers, 36 percent in Croatian rodents, and 37.5 percent in Slovakian rodents.
analysis_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: A comprehensive clinical review by Pencole and colleagues evaluating sixty-eight congenital cases demonstrated that manifestations are dominated by chorioretinitis in 84 percent of cases, hydrocephalus in 53 percent, microcephaly in 31 percent, ventriculomegaly in 16 percent, and periventricular calcifications in 16 percent.
analysis_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 由于治疗措施仍然受到限制,公共卫生战略强调通过综合啮齿动物控制计划进行一级预防,使用湿法清洁技术抑制空气中的气溶胶安全处置家庭感染,以及使用个人防护设备。
